beats.narration: Begin by framing Pipeline Foundation as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages. Consider this worked case: Vertex data enters the pipeline first, where vertex shaders modify position, color, or normal attributes before downstream stages. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Pipeline Foundation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a left-to-right flowchart showing vertex input → vertex shader → primitive assembly → clipping → rasterization → fragment shader → framebuffer.

beats.narration: Now define Primitive Assembly precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles. Consider this worked case: Three connected vertices form a triangle primitive, which the pipeline then processes as a single geometric unit for rendering. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Primitive Assembly
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a wireframe triangle with labeled vertices, highlighting how three points are bound into a single primitive before clipping.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Clipping Stage operates in a concrete sequence. Clipping removes portions outside the view volume. Consider this worked case: A triangle extending beyond the camera's frustum is sliced at the clipping plane boundaries, discarding the exterior segments. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Clipping Stage
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a 3D cube partially outside a transparent viewing box, with clipped edges highlighted in red and retained portions in blue.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Rasterization and make the decision criteria explicit. Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates. Consider this worked case: Each triangle is subdivided into pixel-aligned fragments, with each fragment receiving interpolated attributes for downstream processing. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Rasterization
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a grid overlay on a triangle, showing how each pixel cell becomes a fragment candidate with assigned vertex attributes.

beats.narration: Apply Interpolation to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs. Consider this worked case: Color and normal values are linearly interpolated across a triangle's pixels using barycentric coordinates to ensure smooth shading. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Interpolation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a color gradient across a triangle, with interpolation weights labeled at each vertex and midpoint to show value distribution.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Fragment Processing, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Fragment processing computes values for framebuffer operations. Consider this worked case: Fragment shaders evaluate lighting equations and material properties to generate final color and alpha values for each pixel. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Fragment Processing
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a side-by-side comparison of a raw triangle mesh and its shaded output, with a callout box explaining the fragment shader's role.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Depth Testing with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values. Consider this worked case: Each fragment's depth value is compared against the depth buffer; fragments with greater depth are discarded to maintain correct occlusion. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Depth Testing
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate two overlapping triangles with depth values, highlighting the front triangle as retained and the back triangle as rejected by depth testing.

beats.narration: Use Blending to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Blending combines a fragment result with an existing framebuffer value. Consider this worked case: Translucent surfaces blend the new fragment's color with the underlying color using alpha values to produce semi-transparent overlays. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Blending
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Render a semi-transparent square over a solid background, with a legend showing the blending equation and resulting composite color.

beats.narration: Connect Coordinate Spaces to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit. Consider this worked case: Explicitly defining vertex, fragment, and texture coordinate spaces prevents misalignment during sampling and ensures consistent precision across pipeline stages. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Coordinate Spaces
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a diagram of three nested coordinate spaces (world, view, clip) with labeled axes, emphasizing explicit mapping between them.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error. Consider this worked case: Instructor-led review checks that coordinate mappings are explicit, sampling rates match resolution requirements, and error bounds remain within acceptable thresholds. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a checklist graphic with four boxes: explicit conventions, sampling decisions, measurable error, and coordinate space alignment, each with a tick mark for verification.

sources.excerpt: Computer graphics uses geometric models to represent objects and scenes. Transformations position and orient geometry within coordinate systems. Viewing maps a scene through a camera model to an image. Rasterization samples projected primitives on a discrete pixel grid. Shading models how light, material, and geometry determine appearance. Texture mapping associates image data with geometric surfaces. Curves and surfaces provide compact smooth shape representations. Animation changes scene state over time. Ray tracing follows visibility and light paths through a scene. Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error.
